new_quiz.q: What is an IDE?
choices: A file that stores the settings of a project
The program where you write, build and debug code
A plugin that adds C++ to Blueprints
A window of the Unreal editor that shows errors
new_quiz.explain: An IDE, such as Visual Studio, is the program for working with code. You write the code there, build it, and look for bugs with its debugger.

new_quiz.q: What does it mean that a project compiles?
choices: The code is turned into a program
The assets are saved to disk
The project is uploaded to a server
The levels are loaded into memory
new_quiz.explain: The computer cannot run C++ text directly. Compiling turns your code into a program, and nothing in C++ works until this step succeeds.

new_quiz.q: What is a workload in the IDE?
choices: The time a build takes
The number of files in a project
A list of bugs that must be fixed
A set of extra tools that the IDE needs for a kind of work
new_quiz.explain: The IDE installs tools in sets called workloads. The Epic setup page lists the workloads that Unreal Engine needs on your platform.

new_quiz.q: How does a Blueprint project become a C++ project?
choices: You rename the project folder
You enable a plugin named C++
You add a C++ class with Tools, then New C++ Class
You open the project in a newer engine version
new_quiz.explain: Adding the first C++ class gives the project source code. From then on it is a C++ project and can be built in the IDE.

new_quiz.q: Which configuration do you use when you build the Editor target?
choices: Development Editor
Shipping
Test
Release Server
new_quiz.explain: Development Editor builds your code for use inside the Unreal editor. It is the configuration for daily work.

new_quiz.q: What is the debugger?
choices: The window that lists the assets of the project
The tool that lets you pause the program and look inside it
The tool that installs the workloads
The log that the editor writes to disk
new_quiz.explain: With the debugger you can stop the running program on a line and read the values of its variables.

new_quiz.q: Why do you start the Unreal editor from the IDE in this quest?
choices: The editor cannot be started in any other way
The editor then opens without any levels
The editor then skips compiling
The debugger is then attached, so it can stop the editor on your breakpoint
new_quiz.explain: A breakpoint only works when the debugger watches the program. Starting the editor from the IDE attaches the debugger from the first moment.

new_quiz.q: What is a breakpoint in the IDE?
choices: A line that the compiler skips
An error that stops the build
A mark on a line where the program will pause
A comment that explains a line
new_quiz.explain: When the program reaches the marked line, the debugger pauses it there. You then see that the line ran and what the values are.

new_quiz.q: You set a breakpoint in your class, but the program never stops there. What do you check first?
choices: That the line with the breakpoint is really run, for example by using your class in the level
That the project has a Sky Light
That the IDE window is maximized
That the class name is written in capital letters
new_quiz.explain: A breakpoint only triggers when its line runs. If nothing in the game uses your class, the line is never reached.

new_quiz.q: In which order do you do the first build?
choices: Build the Editor target, then install the IDE, then create the project
Generate the project files, open the solution in the IDE, then build the Editor target
Open the solution, then delete the project files, then start the editor
Start the editor, then install the workloads, then generate the project files
new_quiz.explain: The project files tell the IDE what belongs to the project. With them generated, you open the solution and build.

new_quiz.q: What is reflection in Unreal Engine?
choices: The mirror image of a mesh on a shiny floor
A tool that copies C++ code into Blueprints
The system that lets the editor and Blueprints see C++ code that is marked with macros
A log that lists every compiled class
new_quiz.explain: Plain C++ is invisible to the editor. The macros give Unreal the information it needs to show your classes, variables and functions.

new_quiz.q: Which macro marks a variable for reflection?
choices: UCLASS
UFUNCTION
UENUM
UPROPERTY
new_quiz.explain: UPROPERTY marks a variable. UCLASS marks a class and UFUNCTION marks a function.

new_quiz.q: What are specifiers?
choices: The words inside the macros that decide what the editor and Blueprints may see and change
The names of the C++ files of a class
The errors that the compiler prints
The comments above a function
new_quiz.explain: Specifiers such as EditAnywhere or BlueprintCallable are written inside the macro. Each one grants a certain kind of access.

new_quiz.q: What does the specifier EditAnywhere do?
choices: The property is hidden in the editor
The property can be edited in the Details panel
The property can only be changed in C++
The property is saved to the log
new_quiz.explain: EditAnywhere shows the property in the Details panel and lets you change its value there.

new_quiz.q: A property uses VisibleAnywhere. What is different about it in the Details panel?
choices: It does not appear at all
It appears twice
It is shown, but you cannot edit it
It can be edited only while the game runs
new_quiz.explain: VisibleAnywhere lets you see the value in the Details panel, but not change it. EditAnywhere is the specifier that allows editing.

new_quiz.q: What does the specifier BlueprintReadWrite do?
choices: It lets Blueprint graphs get and set the property
It lets Blueprint graphs delete the property
It writes the property to a file
It makes the property read-only in C++
new_quiz.explain: With BlueprintReadWrite, a Blueprint graph can read the value and also change it.

new_quiz.q: What does UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable) do for a function?
choices: The function runs on every frame
The function can only be called from C++
The function is removed from the class in Blueprints
The function can be called from a Blueprint graph
new_quiz.explain: BlueprintCallable makes the function appear as a node. A Blueprint, such as a child of your class, can then call it.

new_quiz.q: You add a float variable to your class with no UPROPERTY macro. What happens in the editor?
choices: It appears in the Details panel as read-only
It does not appear in the editor
It appears in every Blueprint as a node
It causes a compile error
new_quiz.explain: The editor only knows what reflection tells it. A variable without UPROPERTY is normal C++ and stays invisible to the editor and to Blueprints.

new_quiz.q: How do you create the C++ actor class in the editor?
choices: With Add, then Blueprint Class
With Edit, then Plugins
With Tools, then New C++ Class
With Window, then Output Log
new_quiz.explain: New C++ Class in the Tools menu creates the files of the class and adds them to the project.

new_quiz.q: How do you test your BlueprintCallable function in this quest?
choices: A Blueprint child of your class calls it on BeginPlay
The Level Blueprint calls it on every frame
The IDE calls it during the build
A console command calls it from the Output Log
new_quiz.explain: You make a Blueprint child of the class, call the function on BeginPlay, and place the Blueprint in a level. The log line shows that the call reached your C++ code.

new_quiz.q: What is a BlueprintImplementableEvent?
choices: A function that a Blueprint calls and C++ fills in
A function that C++ calls but only a Blueprint fills in
A function that can only run in the editor
A function with a default version written in C++
new_quiz.explain: C++ decides when the event is called. What happens then is written only in a Blueprint.

new_quiz.q: What is a BlueprintNativeEvent?
choices: A function that cannot be changed by Blueprints
A function that only exists in the Level Blueprint
A function that runs before the game starts
A function with a default version written in C++ that a Blueprint may replace
new_quiz.explain: The C++ version gives a default behavior. A Blueprint child can override it when it needs something else.

new_quiz.q: How do you name the C++ version of the BlueprintNativeEvent OnReset?
choices: OnReset_Implementation
OnReset_Native
OnReset_Default
OnReset_Blueprint
new_quiz.explain: The C++ body of a BlueprintNativeEvent is a function with _Implementation at the end of its name.

new_quiz.q: For which of the two kinds of event do you write no body in C++?
choices: For both of them
For neither of them
For the BlueprintImplementableEvent
For the BlueprintNativeEvent
new_quiz.explain: A BlueprintImplementableEvent is only declared in C++. Its content comes from the Blueprint that implements it.

new_quiz.q: A Blueprint child does not implement OnActivated. What happens when C++ calls it?
choices: The editor crashes
Nothing happens
The C++ default version runs
The Blueprint is deleted
new_quiz.explain: A BlueprintImplementableEvent has no C++ version. With no Blueprint implementation, the call does nothing.

new_quiz.q: A Blueprint child does not override OnReset. What happens when C++ calls it?
choices: Nothing happens
The call is skipped with a warning
The game pauses
The C++ version runs and writes its line to the log
new_quiz.explain: A BlueprintNativeEvent falls back to its C++ version. That is the default behavior you wrote in OnReset_Implementation.

new_quiz.q: In the Blueprint override of OnReset you call the parent version one time. What does the log show?
choices: That both the C++ code and the Blueprint code ran
That only the Blueprint code ran
That only the C++ code ran
That neither of them ran
new_quiz.explain: The override runs the Blueprint nodes, and the call to the parent runs the C++ version. Both leave their mark in the log.

new_quiz.q: You override OnReset in the Blueprint and do not call the parent version. What happens to the C++ version?
choices: It runs before the Blueprint version
It runs after the Blueprint version
It does not run
It runs two times
new_quiz.explain: An override replaces the default. The C++ version only runs if the Blueprint calls the parent version.

new_quiz.q: What is a Blueprint child of your C++ actor?
choices: A copy of the C++ files in another folder
A Blueprint made from your C++ class
A component that is attached to the actor
A level that contains the actor
new_quiz.explain: The Blueprint child has your C++ class as its parent. It gets the events of the class and can implement or override them.

new_quiz.q: When is a BlueprintNativeEvent the better choice?
choices: When Blueprints must never change the behavior
When the function has no use in the game
When C++ has nothing to do at that moment
When there is a sensible default behavior in C++ that designers may want to change
new_quiz.explain: The default lives in C++ and works without any Blueprint. Designers can still replace or extend it without asking a programmer.

new_quiz.q: What is a component?
choices: A part that you add to an actor to give it a shape or a behavior
A level that is loaded inside another level
A file that stores the settings of the editor
A node that connects two Blueprints
new_quiz.explain: A mesh, a collision box and a script that spins the actor are all components. An actor is built from such parts.

new_quiz.q: What is the main gain of writing a behavior as a component?
choices: The behavior runs without an actor
The behavior needs no compiling
You write it once and reuse it on many actors
The behavior cannot be changed by others
new_quiz.explain: A spin component can be added to any actor. The code exists once, and every actor that needs it gets the same behavior.

new_quiz.q: What is the constructor of a class?
choices: The function that runs every frame
The function that runs when the object is created
The function that runs when the game ends
The function that runs when the player presses a key
new_quiz.explain: The constructor sets up a new object. For an actor, it is the place where the default components are created.

new_quiz.q: Which function creates a component in the constructor of an actor?
choices: SetupAttachment
BeginPlay
SpawnActor
CreateDefaultSubobject
new_quiz.explain: CreateDefaultSubobject creates a component that belongs to the actor from the start. You call it once for each component.

new_quiz.q: What do you use SetupAttachment for?
choices: To attach the components to each other
To create a new component
To make a component tick
To show a component in the Details panel
new_quiz.explain: SetupAttachment says which component is the parent of another. The mesh and the box then follow the root scene component.

new_quiz.q: Why do you mark the components with UPROPERTY(VisibleAnywhere)?
choices: So they are deleted when the game starts
So they tick every frame
So you can see them in the editor
So they cannot be attached
new_quiz.explain: Without UPROPERTY the editor does not know the components. VisibleAnywhere shows them in the editor, where you can then set their properties.

new_quiz.q: Which class is your own spin component based on?
choices: AActor
UActorComponent
AGameModeBase
UUserWidget
new_quiz.explain: UActorComponent is the base class for components that add behavior. A class such as UUSpinComponent builds on it.

new_quiz.q: What does it mean that a component ticks?
choices: It is created in the constructor
It is attached to the root
It is visible in the Details panel
It runs every frame
new_quiz.explain: A tick is one update per frame. The spin component uses it to rotate a little on every frame.

new_quiz.q: What does the spin component rotate?
choices: Its owner, the actor it belongs to
The camera of the player
Every actor in the level
Only itself, and nothing that is visible
new_quiz.explain: A component can reach the actor it is added to, which is its owner. Rotating the owner makes the whole actor spin.

new_quiz.q: You added your spin component to a Blueprint actor, but the actor does not move in the game. What do you check first in the component?
choices: That its name starts with BP_
That it is marked VisibleAnywhere
That it is set to tick
That it has a static mesh
new_quiz.explain: The rotation happens in the tick of the component. If ticking is not turned on for the component, that code never runs.

new_quiz.q: What is Live Coding?
choices: A stream that shows your screen to other people
A tool that writes C++ code for you
A feature that compiles your C++ changes while the editor is still open
A mode that runs the game without compiling
new_quiz.explain: With Live Coding you change the code and apply it without closing the editor. It saves the time of a restart.

new_quiz.q: Which shortcut applies a change with Live Coding?
choices: Ctrl+Alt+F11
Ctrl+B
F9
Shift+P
new_quiz.explain: Ctrl+Alt+F11 starts a Live Coding compile while the editor stays open.

new_quiz.q: What is the body of a function?
choices: The name of the function
The file the function is saved in
The list of its inputs
The code inside the function
new_quiz.explain: The body is the code that runs when the function is called. The name and the inputs are not part of the body.

new_quiz.q: Which kind of change is the safest to apply with Live Coding?
choices: Adding a new UPROPERTY to a class
Changing the body of a function
Changing the parent of a class
Removing a variable from a class
new_quiz.explain: A changed function body does not change what the class looks like to the editor. Only the code that runs is replaced.

new_quiz.q: After which change is it safer to close the editor and build again from the IDE?
choices: After changing a number inside a function body
After changing a log text inside a function body
After adding a new UPROPERTY to your class
After reading the code with no change
new_quiz.explain: A new UPROPERTY changes the class itself and its reflection data. The open editor still holds the old form of the class, which can cause strange bugs.

new_quiz.q: What are the steps of a full rebuild in this quest?
choices: Close the editor, build the project from the IDE, and open the editor again
Press Ctrl+Alt+F11 two times
Delete the class and write it again
Save all levels and press Play
new_quiz.explain: With the editor closed, the IDE builds everything fresh. When the editor opens again, it loads the new version of every class.

new_quiz.q: What can happen if you keep working after a change that needed a restart?
choices: The IDE removes your code
The project is deleted
The editor refuses to open any level
You can get bugs that are very hard to understand
new_quiz.explain: The editor and your code no longer agree about the class. The result can be wrong values or crashes that have no clear cause.

new_quiz.q: What is the gain of Live Coding when the change is safe?
choices: The game runs faster
It is fast, because the editor does not have to restart
The code needs no testing
The project gets smaller
new_quiz.explain: A restart costs time on every change. For safe changes, Live Coding lets you test a few seconds after you edit.

new_quiz.q: A property you just added with Live Coding shows strange values in the editor. What do you do first?
choices: Add the property a second time
Rename the project
Close the editor, build from the IDE, and open the editor again
Delete the Blueprint children of the class
new_quiz.explain: The strange values are a sign that the editor holds old data for the class. A full rebuild with the editor closed brings both back in line.

new_quiz.q: What does the rule that you write for this quest say?
choices: Which changes are safe to apply with Live Coding and which need a restart
How many classes a project may have
Which IDE is the fastest
How often the editor must be updated
new_quiz.explain: Your rule tells you when to trust Live Coding and when to restart. You give one example of each case.
